title: Burning chest pain after meals in a 45-year-old basketball coach
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 45-year-old woman in the ED with 4 weeks of burning central chest pain that is worse lying down and after meals, who fears a heart attack because her father died of one. The candidate then interprets her observations, ECG, serial high-sensitivity troponin and bloods, recognises that acute MI is excluded and that she is low risk for ACS, recognises reflux with alarm features, and outlines management, the complications of reflux, and safety netting.
focus: Separating reflux from acute coronary syndrome in ED chest pain, and recognising the alarm features that need a gastroscopy
context: Family history of premature coronary disease
diagnosis: Acute MI excluded; low risk for ACS on serial high-sensitivity troponin
stem: You are a final-year medical student in the Emergency Department of a metropolitan hospital. Kelly Morrison, a 45-year-old woman, has come in tonight with chest pain. The ED registrar has asked you to assess her. She is on a trolley in the acute area. A nurse is with you: she has taken Kelly's observations and recorded an ECG, and she can carry out your instructions.
tasks: Take a focused history from Kelly and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you her observations, her ECG and her blood results, including serial troponin. Give an ISBAR handover with your interpretation, your diagnosis and differentials, your management and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Kelly Morrison, a 45-year-old professional basketball coach. You are sitting up on the trolley with a hand over the middle of your chest. You are frightened and talk quickly, because you are sure this is your heart. You calm down if the candidate takes your fear seriously and explains things in plain words. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they would examine.

What the nurse reports at the start (if the candidate asks, or straight away if they do not): "Her obs are all in the white zone: heart rate 96 and regular, BP 142/88, resps 18, sats 98% on room air, temp 36.7. Pain is 7 out of 10. I did an ECG at 21:38 and the registrar has looked at it. Bloods, including a troponin, are going off now." If the candidate asks to see the ECG or the bloods, the examiner says they will be given in Part 2.

How you change with what the candidate does:

  • The pain eases by itself over the 10 minutes, to about 4/10 by the end of Part 1, as your episodes always do.
  • If the candidate offers pain relief, an antacid or aspirin, the nurse says she will ask the registrar to chart it; nothing is given before Part 2.
  • If the candidate offers GTN, the nurse says she will ask the registrar to chart it; it is not given before Part 2.
  • If the candidate rushes past your fear or uses jargon, you get more anxious and say, "So it is my heart?"

Opening line: "The last month I've been getting this terrible chest pain. It's happening more and more often and it's freaking me out!"

History (give only when asked):

The pain

  • Site: point to the middle of your breastbone.
  • Onset: the first episode was 4 weeks ago, while you were lying down watching TV before bed. Tonight it started at about 8:45 pm, on the couch after a big takeaway dinner.
  • Character: "It feels like a burning sensation."
  • Radiation: none. It does not go to the arm, jaw, neck or back.
  • Duration and course: each episode lasts 1 to 2 hours, then fades away. At first it came once or twice a week; now it comes most nights.
  • Worse: "It's worse when I'm lying down and after I eat any meal. It's really frustrating."
  • Better: sitting up helps a little. You have not tried any antacids or other tablets.
  • Exertion (only if asked): it has never come on while walking, climbing stairs or running drills on court, and rest does not bring it on or take it away.
  • Severity: 7/10.
  • Impact: "It's stressing me out. I need this sorted." You are sleeping badly.

Other symptoms (only if asked)

  • Positive: a sour, acid taste coming up into your throat, mostly at night or when you bend over. Over the last couple of weeks, solid food like bread or steak sometimes feels as if it sticks behind your breastbone and you have to wash it down with water. Drinks go down fine. You have lost about 5 kg over the last 3 months without trying – your clothes are looser.
  • Negative: no breathlessness, sweating, nausea, fainting or palpitations with the pain. No separate pain in the upper tummy; the pain is behind the breastbone. No vomiting, no vomiting blood, no black or tarry stools. No bloating or feeling full early. No sudden mouthfuls of watery saliva (water brash). No lump in the throat, no food coming back up undigested, you do not eat slowly. No hoarseness, no cough, no bad breath, no hiccups. No fevers, night sweats, rigors or tiredness beyond poor sleep. No lumps in your neck that you have noticed. No leg pain or swelling.

Past medical history

  • Mild depression, managed with CBT with a psychologist. It has been stable.
  • No operations and no hospital admissions. No known high blood pressure, diabetes or high cholesterol, though you "haven't had a check-up in years".
  • Immunisations up to date.

Medications

  • Sertraline once a day. If asked the dose, say it is the lowest one and you cannot remember the number.
  • Mirena (hormonal IUD) for contraception.
  • No over-the-counter medicines: no anti-inflammatories, no aspirin, no antacids. No recent antibiotics. No vitamins or supplements. No recreational drugs.

Allergies: dust. No drug allergies.

Family history

  • Mother: asthma.
  • Father: died of a heart attack at 50.
  • No siblings.

Social history

  • Smoking: never smoked.
  • Alcohol: "a few drinks to unwind." If asked to be specific: about 4 standard drinks every day, usually wine or beer after training or games.
  • Occupation: professional basketball coach.
  • Exercise: you walk for 30 minutes once a week. You coach from the sideline and run drills, but you do not train yourself.
  • Diet: poor. You are always on the go for work and eat a lot of takeaway, often late at night.
  • Living situation: you are always travelling for work, on short interstate trips with the team. No long-haul or overseas travel recently.
  • Support: solid. Your partner and friends are very supportive.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: "I think I'm having a heart attack. My dad died of one at about my age and it terrifies me." Your concern is that you will die. You want to know for sure whether it is your heart, and you want this sorted out.

Question to ask in Part 1 (once, partway through): "Am I having a heart attack? Just tell me."

Exam findings (give only when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General: alert, anxious woman sitting upright, comfortable at rest apart from the pain. Not pale, jaundiced or sweaty. Weight 82 kg (previously about 87 kg), height 168 cm (BMI 29). Observations as the nurse reported.
  • Hands: warm, CRT 2 seconds. No clubbing, no koilonychia, no palmar erythema, no tar staining.
  • Pulse and BP: 96/min and regular. Radial pulses equal, no radio-radial delay. BP right arm 142/88, left arm 140/86.
  • Face and eyes: no conjunctival pallor, no scleral icterus, no xanthelasma or corneal arcus.
  • Neck: JVP not raised. No cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, including the left supraclavicular fossa. Thyroid normal.
  • Heart: apex beat not displaced. Dual heart sounds, no murmurs, no added sounds, no pericardial rub.
  • Chest wall: no tenderness. Palpation does not reproduce the pain.
  • Lungs: equal expansion, resonant, clear breath sounds, no crackles or wheeze.
  • Abdomen: soft and not distended. Mild epigastric tenderness with no guarding or rebound. No masses, no hepatomegaly or splenomegaly, Murphy's sign negative. No spider naevi, caput medusae or other signs of chronic liver disease.
  • Rectal examination (if the candidate asks): brown stool on the glove, no melaena.
  • Legs: no oedema. Calves soft, non-tender and equal.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self as a medical student, confirms Kelly's identity and explains that the registrar asked them to assess her.
Acknowledges her fear of a heart attack and her father's death with empathy, does not dismiss it before the results are back, uses plain language, and asks about alcohol without judgement.
History
Characterises the chest pain:

kids.x: Site: central retrosternal, with no radiation
Onset 4 weeks ago while lying watching TV; burning in character; severity 7/10
Episodes last 1 to 2 hours and are becoming more frequent (now most nights)
Worse lying down and after meals, eased a little by sitting up; tonight's episode came on after a large meal

check.x: Asks about features of cardiac ischaemia, including pain on exertion and relief with rest plus at least three of: radiation to the arm, jaw or neck, breathlessness, sweating, nausea, syncope, palpitations (all negative).
Asks about reflux symptoms: acid regurgitation (positive, at night and on bending), water brash, nocturnal cough, hoarseness and halitosis.
Asks about alarm features:

kids.x: Dysphagia: solids sticking behind the sternum for 2 weeks, liquids fine
Unintentional weight loss: about 5 kg (about 6%) over 3 months
GI bleeding: haematemesis and black or tarry stools (none)
Persistent vomiting, early satiety, night sweats or fevers (none)

check.x: Asks about features of the other gastrointestinal differentials: epigastric pain and bloating (peptic ulcer), NSAID, aspirin or recent antibiotic use (ulcer or pill oesophagitis), and globus, regurgitation of undigested food or slow eating (motility disorder).
Takes the past history, medications and allergies: mild depression managed with CBT, sertraline, Mirena, no over-the-counter medicines or supplements, no previous operations, allergy to dust only.
Takes the family history and recognises premature coronary disease: father died of a heart attack at 50 (mother has asthma).
Asks about cardiovascular risk factors: smoking (never), known hypertension, diabetes or high cholesterol (none known; no check-up in years), exercise (walks once a week) and diet (poor, takeaway).
Quantifies alcohol beyond "a few drinks" (about 4 standard drinks daily, 28 a week) and asks about work, frequent travel with the team, recreational drugs and support.
Explores her ideas, concerns and expectations: thinks it is a heart attack like her father's, fears dying, wants it resolved.
Examination
General inspection and vital signs, including pallor, distress, sweating and weight or BMI.
Cardiovascular examination: pulse rate and rhythm, radial pulses and BP in both arms, JVP, heart sounds, murmurs, pericardial rub and peripheral oedema.
Palpates the chest wall for reproducible tenderness and auscultates the lungs.
Examines the abdomen: epigastric tenderness (mild), masses, hepatomegaly and signs of chronic liver disease.
Looks for signs of malignancy and anaemia: cervical and left supraclavicular lymph nodes, conjunctival pallor and koilonychia.
Asks to review the 12-lead ECG now and requests serial high-sensitivity troponin on the local assay-specific pathway (e.g. 0 and 1 h or 0 and 2 h).
Asks for the ECG to be repeated with any change in pain.
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: every value is in the white zone, so no clinical review or rapid response is triggered; HR falls and pain settles over about 2 hours without specific treatment, matching her usual 1 to 2 hour episodes.
Interprets the ECG: sinus rhythm with normal axis and intervals, no ST or T wave change during pain and no change on the repeat. States that a normal ECG alone does not exclude ACS.

Interprets the troponin: hs-troponin I 3 ng/L at 0 and 2 hours, below the assay's female 99th percentile (16 ng/L on this assay) with no rise, so acute myocardial infarction is excluded and she is low risk for ACS.
Interprets the other bloods: normal Hb (no anaemia), normal lipase, CRP and transaminases; a raised GGT (74) and MCV (101) are in keeping with her alcohol intake.

Gives the diagnosis as gastro-oesophageal reflux disease with alarm features (dysphagia and unintentional weight loss), justified by burning retrosternal pain that is worse lying down and after meals, with acid regurgitation and no exertional features.
Gives at least three differentials, each with a feature for or against: ACS or unstable angina, peptic ulcer disease, an oesophageal motility disorder, and oesophageal or gastric cancer.
Management
Explains in plain words that the heart tests show no heart attack, acknowledges her father's history, and explains that reflux of stomach acid is the likely cause.
Plans discharge from the ED as low risk, without admission, with a GP letter, and advises avoiding NSAIDs (especially with sertraline, which together raise upper GI bleeding risk).
Gives lifestyle advice:

kids.x: Elevate the head of the bed, avoid lying down within 2 to 3 hours of eating, and eat smaller meals
Avoid her trigger foods and drinks (for example spicy or fatty food, coffee, chocolate, citrus, fizzy drinks)
Cut alcohol to within the NHMRC guideline (no more than 10 standard drinks a week and no more than 4 on any day) with a brief intervention; weight loss and more exercise

check.x: Starts a standard-dose PPI once daily 30–60 minutes before breakfast for 4–8 weeks (e.g. pantoprazole 40 mg or esomeprazole 20 mg).
Antacid or alginate for breakthrough; review and step down; H2RA as an alternative.
Refers for urgent (Category 1, within 30 days, ideally sooner) gastroscopy because of the dysphagia and weight loss, and does not rely on a PPI trial first.
Mentions Helicobacter pylori testing (biopsy at gastroscopy).
Asks the GP to assess her cardiovascular risk (BP, lipids, glucose or HbA1c, absolute risk with her premature family history) and to arrange further cardiac testing if exertional symptoms appear.

Names at least three complications of reflux that the gastroscopy looks for: erosive oesophagitis (with bleeding), peptic stricture, Barrett's oesophagus, oesophageal adenocarcinoma (may be earned in Q3 or Q4).
Safety netting

Tells Kelly in plain words to call 000 for chest pain that is different from her usual burning, naming at least three of: spreads to the arm, jaw or neck; comes on with exertion; breathlessness, sweating or faintness; more severe or not settling as usual.

Tells her to return to ED the same day for at least two of: vomiting blood, black stools, food stuck completely, unable to swallow liquids, and arranges GP review within about a week and the gastroscopy appointment.

part2.lead: Here are her observations over the last two hours, her ECGs and her blood results, including the 2-hour troponin.
part2.patient: If the candidate gives vague reassurance ("it's nothing"), say: "Then why does it keep happening?"

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Room air throughout. Sitting up on the trolley. Pain scores as reported by Kelly.
handover.model:
• Read: RR 16 to 18, SpO2 98 to 99% on room air, BP 142/88 falling to 128/80, HR 96 falling to 78 and regular, temperature 36.7 to 36.8 °C, alert: every value is in the white zone at every time point. Pain falls from 7/10 to 1/10 by 22:45 and 0/10 by 23:45.
  • Meaning: she is haemodynamically stable with no chart calling criterion. The early tachycardia and higher BP fit pain and anxiety. The pain settles over about 2 hours without specific treatment, matching her usual 1 to 2 hour episodes.
  • Changes: no clinical review or rapid response is needed, so the plan is the chest pain pathway (serial ECG and troponin) and then discharge if she is low risk. Repeat the ECG and observations if the pain returns or changes.

rows.note: Triage ATS 2 chest pain; ECG to be done now. No analgesia or antacid given.
Repeat set; pain easing; repeat ECG done. Registrar reviewed; analgesia offered, Kelly declined as pain settling.

handover.label: 12-lead ECG (on arrival and repeat)
handover.result:
12-lead ECG at 21:38 (25 mm/s, 10 mm/mV), recorded during pain 7/10

  • Rate: 94/min.
  • Rhythm: sinus rhythm; regular, with a P wave before every QRS.
  • Axis: normal, about +50°.
  • PR interval: 152 ms.
  • QRS duration: 86 ms.
  • QTc: 418 ms (Bazett).
  • ST segments: isoelectric in all leads. No ST elevation or depression.
  • T waves: upright in I, II, aVL, aVF and V2 to V6; inverted in aVR and V1 only.
  • Other: no pathological Q waves, normal R wave progression, no bundle branch block, no LVH by voltage criteria.

Conclusion: sinus rhythm; normal ECG with no acute ischaemic change.

Repeat 12-lead ECG at 22:45 (pain 1/10): sinus rhythm 82/min, no change from the 21:38 tracing. Conclusion: unchanged; no dynamic ST or T wave change.

Comparison: no previous ECG on file.
handover.model:
• Read: sinus rhythm 94/min with a normal axis, PR, QRS and QTc. No ST elevation or depression, T wave inversion only in aVR and V1 (normal), no Q waves, no bundle branch block, no LVH. The repeat tracing an hour later is unchanged, and there is no old ECG to compare.
  • Meaning: a normal ECG recorded during 7/10 pain makes active ischaemia less likely, and no dynamic change on the repeat is reassuring. But a normal ECG alone does not exclude ACS, so the troponin results are needed.
  • Changes: no STEMI pathway. Continue the chest pain pathway with serial hs-troponin, and repeat the ECG if the pain comes back or changes.

handover.label: Bloods, including serial high-sensitivity troponin
handover.result: First sample collected 21:45, about 1 hour after the pain began at 20:45. Second troponin collected 23:45.
handover.model:
• Read: hs-troponin I 3 ng/L at 0 hours and 3 ng/L at 2 hours: both well below the assay's female 99th percentile (16 ng/L on this assay), with no change between them. Hb 128 g/L, normal. MCV 101 fL, mildly raised. WCC, platelets, electrolytes, creatinine, CRP and lipase normal. Bilirubin, ALT, ALP and albumin normal; GGT 74 U/L raised.
  • Meaning: no myocardial injury. With a low clinical risk score (TIMI 0, EDACS low), a non-ischaemic ECG, serial troponin very low and unchanged, acute MI is excluded and she is low risk for ACS. A normal Hb means no anaemia from occult bleeding. A normal lipase and CRP argue against pancreatitis and an inflammatory cause. A raised GGT and MCV with normal transaminases fit her alcohol intake, a reflux risk factor.
  • Changes: she can be discharged from the ED with outpatient follow-up. Raise the alcohol with her, and send a GP letter covering the GGT and MCV and her cardiovascular risk.

rows.n: Assay-specific 99th percentile: female 16 ng/L, male 34 ng/L.

ask: You are now handing over to the ED registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Kelly Morrison, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Kelly now, here in the emergency department, and the treatment plan for when she goes home.
Kelly asks you, "So it's not my heart? Then why do I need a camera test?" Please answer her, then tell her what to watch for and what follow-up you will arrange.
expect:
• Identify: self, final-year medical student; Kelly Morrison, 45, in ED.
  • Situation: 4 weeks of recurrent burning retrosternal pain; tonight's episode has settled; acute MI excluded and low risk for ACS; likely reflux with alarm features.
  • Background: worse lying down and after meals, lasts 1 to 2 hours, acid regurgitation, no exertional features; solid dysphagia for 2 weeks and 5 kg unintentional weight loss over 3 months; about 4 standard drinks daily; father died of MI at 50; depression on sertraline; Mirena.
  • Assessment: obs white zone throughout; ECG sinus rhythm with no ischaemic change during pain, unchanged on repeat; hs-TnI 3 then 3 ng/L (below 16, no rise); with a low risk score (TIMI 0, EDACS low), MI is excluded and she is low risk; Hb, lipase and CRP normal; GGT 74 and MCV 101 fit alcohol.
  • Recommendation: review for discharge on a PPI with lifestyle advice; urgent gastroscopy referral; GP follow-up for cardiovascular risk.

GORD with alarm features: burning central pain, worse lying down and after meals, acid regurgitation, no exertional component; alcohol and BMI 29 as risk factors; dysphagia and weight loss are the alarm features.

  • ACS or unstable angina (must exclude): for: father died of MI at 50, pain increasing in frequency; against: not exertional, no associated features, normal ECG during pain, serial troponin negative.
  • Peptic ulcer disease: for: worse after meals, mild epigastric tenderness; against: no bloating, NSAIDs or bleeding, normal Hb.
  • Oesophageal motility disorder: for: dysphagia, retrosternal pain; against: solids only, no globus or regurgitation of undigested food.
  • Oesophageal or gastric cancer: for: new dysphagia to solids, 5 kg unintentional weight loss over 3 months, daily alcohol; against: no anaemia, haematemesis, hoarseness or palpable nodes; aged 45 and a non-smoker.

1. In the ED: chest pain pathway completed: low clinical risk score (EDACS <16, TIMI 0), non-ischaemic ECG, hs-troponin at 0 and 2 hours very low and unchanged (rule-out); repeat ECG if pain recurs.
  2. Disposition: low risk, so discharge with a GP letter; no admission.
  3. Lifestyle: head of bed up, nothing to eat for 2 to 3 hours before lying down, smaller meals, avoid triggers, alcohol within NHMRC limits with a brief intervention, weight loss.
  4. Medication: standard-dose PPI before breakfast for 4 to 8 weeks (for example pantoprazole 40 mg), antacid or alginate for breakthrough; H2 receptor antagonist as an alternative; avoid NSAIDs (especially with sertraline: upper GI bleeding risk).
  5. Urgent gastroscopy (Category 1, within 30 days, ideally sooner) for dysphagia and weight loss, with biopsies including for H. pylori.
  6. GP: cardiovascular risk assessment given premature family history.

• Not her heart: heart tests tonight show no heart attack; your GP will still check your heart risk because of your dad.
  • Why the camera test: food sticking and losing weight without trying mean the gullet must be looked at directly rather than just treated with tablets; acid damage can cause inflammation and ulcers that can bleed, narrowing, Barrett's change and rarely cancer.
  • Call 000: chest pain different from her usual burning, at least three of: spreads to the arm, jaw or neck; comes on with exertion; breathlessness, sweating or faintness; more severe or not settling as usual.
  • ED the same day: at least two of: vomiting blood, black stools, food stuck completely, unable to swallow liquids.
  • Follow-up: GP within about a week with the discharge letter; gastroscopy appointment.

ddx.dx: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease with alarm features (dysphagia and unintentional weight loss)
ddx.for: She has 4 weeks of burning retrosternal pain that is worse lying down and after meals, with acid regurgitation, no exertional features, a normal ECG and negative serial troponin.
ddx.against: Dysphagia and weight loss are not explained by uncomplicated reflux and need a gastroscopy to exclude a stricture or cancer.

ddx.dx: Acute coronary syndrome or unstable angina
ddx.for: Her father died of a myocardial infarction at 50, and her chest pain is becoming more frequent.
ddx.against: The pain is burning, positional and related to meals, never exertional and has no associated features, and her ECG during pain and her troponin at 0 and 2 hours are normal.

ddx.for: Her pain is worse after meals, she drinks about 4 standard drinks a day and has mild epigastric tenderness.
ddx.against: The pain is retrosternal rather than epigastric, with no bloating, early satiety, NSAID use or bleeding, and her Hb is normal.

ddx.dx: Oesophageal motility disorder (for example oesophageal spasm or achalasia)
ddx.for: She has retrosternal pain with recent dysphagia.
ddx.against: The dysphagia is to solids only, with no globus, slow eating or regurgitation of undigested food, and the pain is clearly linked to meals and lying flat.

ddx.for: She has new dysphagia to solids, 5 kg unintentional weight loss over 3 months and drinks alcohol daily.
ddx.against: She has no anaemia, haematemesis, hoarseness or palpable lymph nodes, and she is 45 and a non-smoker.

guide:
In Part 1, Kelly answers the history and the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they examine. Volunteer only the opening line and her fear of a heart attack. Give the dysphagia, weight loss and alcohol quantity only when asked. If the candidate asks for the ECG or bloods in Part 1, say they will be given in Part 2. Item 21 is earned when the candidate asks to review the 12-lead ECG now and requests serial high-sensitivity troponin (0/1 h or 0/2 h per local pathway); item 22 when they ask for the ECG to be repeated with any change in pain. Neither is earned by interpreting the ECG. In Part 2, hand over all three results, then ask the four questions in order, reading out Kelly's question for the last one. Kelly says her one scripted line only if the candidate gives vague reassurance.

Do not penalise a candidate who orders aspirin 300 mg early for possible ACS after checking for contraindications, as long as they do not commit to an ACS diagnosis against the results. Equally, do not require it. Accept any standard-dose PPI.

A high-performing candidate takes her fear seriously and rules ACS in or out properly, without being falsely reassuring or anchoring on the heart. They ask cluster questions for cardiac ischaemia, reflux, peptic ulcer, motility disorders and malignancy, and they find the dysphagia and weight loss. They quantify the alcohol and recognise the premature family history. In Part 2 they read the normal ECG and the flat troponin below the female cut-off as excluding MI, diagnose reflux with alarm features, and start a PPI with lifestyle advice. They refer for an urgent gastroscopy rather than a PPI trial alone, name the complications of reflux, and safety-net in plain words for cardiac and GI red flags.

A borderline candidate calls it reflux from the first answer and skips the cardiac questions, or the reverse: never moves on from ACS. They miss the dysphagia and weight loss, accept "a few drinks", or prescribe a PPI and discharge without a gastroscopy referral or GP follow-up for her cardiovascular risk.
explain:
Summary

Kelly has gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD). It has two alarm features, new dysphagia to solids and unintentional weight loss, so she needs an urgent gastroscopy. Any ED chest pain needs ACS excluded first, and her family history adds to her fear and her long-term risk. The ED excludes acute coronary syndrome (ACS) with the ECG and serial high-sensitivity troponin. Then the station turns to treating the reflux and investigating the alarm features.

Excluding ACS in the ED

The 2025 Australian and New Zealand ACS guideline (Heart Foundation and CSANZ) and the ACSQHC Acute Coronary Syndromes Clinical Care Standard call for a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of arrival and assessment of possible ACS on a validated pathway using high-sensitivity troponin. Current guidance uses assay-specific 0/1 h or 0/2 h hs-troponin algorithms; Kelly's very low, unchanged values meet rule-out on either. On such a pathway a patient is low risk when a validated clinical score is low (for example EDACS <16 or TIMI 0), the ECG shows no ischaemia, and serial hs-troponin is below the 99th percentile with no significant change. Kelly's EDACS is low (age 45, female, one risk factor) and her TIMI score is 0. Low-risk patients can be discharged with outpatient follow-up. Kelly's ECG during 7/10 pain was normal and unchanged on repeat, and her hs-troponin I was 3 ng/L at 0 and 2 hours, against this assay's female 99th percentile of 16 ng/L. Acute MI is excluded.

Two traps catch candidates. First, a normal ECG alone never excludes ACS. Second, relief of pain with an antacid or a "GI cocktail" does not distinguish oesophageal from cardiac pain. Oesophageal spasm can also respond to GTN.

The history that makes the diagnosis

Ask cluster questions for each differential.

  • GORD: burning retrosternal pain, worse lying flat and after meals, with acid regurgitation, water brash, cough, hoarseness or halitosis.
  • Oesophagitis: drugs that cause pill oesophagitis (for example doxycycline, NSAIDs, bisphosphonates) and haematemesis.
  • Peptic ulcer disease: epigastric pain related to meals, bloating, early satiety, NSAID use and bleeding.
  • Malignancy: dysphagia, weight loss, night sweats, hoarseness, hiccups, lymph nodes.
  • Motility disorders: dysphagia to solids and liquids, regurgitation of undigested food, slow eating, globus.
  • Stable angina and ACS: pain on exertion relieved by rest, radiation to the neck, jaw or arm, breathlessness, sweating, nausea, syncope.

Her father's death at 50 is premature coronary disease in a first-degree relative. It explains her fear, and it matters for her long-term cardiovascular risk even though tonight's tests are reassuring.

Examination

The examination looks for haemodynamic compromise and cardiac signs (BP in both arms, murmurs, rub, heart failure) and reproducible chest wall tenderness. It also checks for epigastric tenderness and masses, signs of chronic liver disease from alcohol, anaemia, and the left supraclavicular (Virchow's) node of upper GI cancer. Her mild epigastric tenderness keeps peptic ulcer disease on the list.

Interpreting the other results

Her observations were in the white zone throughout, and the pain settled over about 2 hours without specific treatment, in keeping with her usual 1 to 2 hour episodes. Her Hb is normal, so there is no evidence of occult bleeding. A normal lipase and CRP argue against pancreatitis and an inflammatory cause. A raised GGT and macrocytosis with normal transaminases fit her alcohol intake of about 28 standard drinks a week. This is above the NHMRC guideline of no more than 10 standard drinks a week and no more than 4 on any one day, and alcohol is a risk factor for reflux.

Managing GORD (eTG)

  • Lifestyle: raise the head of the bed, avoid eating for 2 to 3 hours before lying down, eat smaller meals, avoid personal triggers (spicy or fatty food, coffee, chocolate, citrus, carbonated drinks), reduce alcohol, stop smoking, and lose weight if overweight (her BMI is 29).
  • Medication: an antacid or alginate for mild, intermittent symptoms. For frequent symptoms, a standard-dose PPI once daily before breakfast (for example esomeprazole 20 mg, omeprazole 20 mg, pantoprazole 40 mg or rabeprazole 20 mg) for 4 to 8 weeks, then step down to the lowest effective dose or on-demand use. An H2 receptor antagonist is an alternative for milder disease. Avoid NSAIDs: taken with an SSRI such as her sertraline, they markedly raise the risk of upper GI bleeding.
  • Surgery: laparoscopic Nissen fundoplication for selected patients whose reflux does not respond to medical therapy or who cannot tolerate a PPI. It is not a decision for tonight, before the gastroscopy.

Alarm features and gastroscopy

Dysphagia, unintentional weight loss, GI bleeding, anaemia and persistent vomiting are alarm features. Any of them calls for prompt upper GI endoscopy rather than an empirical PPI trial alone. Kelly has two. Her loss of about 5 kg (about 6% of her body weight) in 3 months is clinically significant unintentional weight loss (more than 5%). Under Australian endoscopy categorisation, dysphagia with weight loss is Category 1 (within 30 days, ideally sooner). The gastroscopy also allows biopsies, including for Helicobacter pylori, which matters if a peptic ulcer is found. A PPI lowers the yield of H. pylori testing (false negatives) and can heal oesophagitis before the scope, so tell the endoscopist she is on a PPI; histology is preferred for H. pylori, and the PPI may need to be withheld for 2 weeks if non-invasive H. pylori testing is used instead.

Complications of GORD

  • Erosive oesophagitis: can ulcerate and bleed.
  • Peptic stricture: causes dysphagia to solids, but usually follows longer-standing reflux; with only 4 weeks of symptoms, Kelly's new dysphagia and weight loss mean cancer must be excluded at gastroscopy.
  • Barrett's oesophagus: intestinal metaplasia of the lower oesophagus.
  • Oesophageal adenocarcinoma: Barrett's oesophagus is the precursor.

Cardiovascular risk

Tonight's tests exclude MI, but they do not measure her long-term risk. She is 45, which is within the age range of the 2023 Australian cardiovascular disease risk guideline. She has not had her lipids or glucose checked in years, she exercises little, and a premature family history of CVD is a factor that can reclassify her risk upward. Her GP should assess her absolute risk and arrange further cardiac testing if exertional symptoms appear.

Safety netting and follow-up

Tell Kelly in plain words to call 000 for chest pain that is different from her usual burning: pain that spreads to the arm, jaw or neck, comes on with exertion, comes with breathlessness, sweating or faintness, or is more severe, getting worse, or not settling the way her usual episodes do. She should come back to the ED the same day for vomiting blood, black stools, food getting stuck completely, or being unable to swallow liquids, and see her GP sooner if her swallowing worsens or she keeps losing weight. Follow-up is a GP review within about a week with the discharge letter and the gastroscopy appointment. The GP can then review the PPI at 4 to 8 weeks, offer alcohol support, assess her cardiovascular risk, and check her mood, given her depression and the stress this has caused.
points: In ED chest pain, rule out ACS before settling on reflux: a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes, then serial high-sensitivity troponin on a validated assay-specific 0/1 h or 0/2 h pathway. A normal ECG alone does not exclude ACS.
Relief with an antacid or GTN does not distinguish oesophageal pain from cardiac pain.
Burning retrosternal pain that is worse lying down and after meals, with acid regurgitation and no exertional features, points to GORD.
Dysphagia, unintentional weight loss (more than 5% of body weight), GI bleeding, anaemia and persistent vomiting are alarm features. They need a prompt gastroscopy, not just a PPI trial.

Manage GORD with lifestyle change (head of bed up, no late meals, smaller meals, less alcohol, weight loss) and a standard-dose PPI before breakfast for 4 to 8 weeks, then step down. Avoid NSAIDs, especially with an SSRI. Fundoplication is for refractory disease.
The complications of GORD are erosive oesophagitis, peptic stricture, Barrett's oesophagus and oesophageal adenocarcinoma.
